title: Failures, then a successful sign-in
brief: Triage the authentication sequence without assuming that success proves account ownership.
context: You are reviewing an identity alert for {{user}} at fictional organization {{org}}. The case window contains failed authentication followed by a success, but the first alert is only a summary.

initial.text: At {{time}}, {{count}} failed sign-ins for {{user}} were recorded from {{ip}}.
At {{later}}, a successful sign-in from the same source created session {{session}}.
The alert does not include the successful session’s authentication method, device identity, or subsequent activity.

unknowns: Which authentication method and device belong to the successful session?
Do the failures and success represent the same application flow?
Does the account owner recognize the session?
hypotheses: A legitimate client retried stale credentials before the user signed in.
Someone obtained usable credentials and opened a session.
The summary combines unrelated authentication attempts.

checks.label: Correlate the successful session
checks.purpose: Inspect the actual authentication and device records.
checks.scope: Account {{user}}, session {{session}}, case time window only.

checks.label: Review session activity and owner confirmation
checks.purpose: Compare recorded activity with independently collected owner confirmation.
checks.scope: Session {{session}} and the associated analyst confirmation record.

checks.label: Read the tenant’s daily sign-in totals
checks.purpose: See general volume; aggregate totals cannot identify this session’s actor.
checks.scope: Read-only daily totals for {{org}}.

results: The successful session used phishing-resistant MFA on the user’s registered managed device. The failures came from a stale client credential cache.
The recorded session stayed within the user’s usual application, and an independently recorded owner callback confirms the sign-in.
The tenant had routine successes and failures during the day. The aggregate report contains no session identifiers or attribution for this case.
variants.reasoning: Session correlation and owner confirmation support a legitimate explanation for this sequence. They reduce concern without proving every associated action was safe.
remaining: Whether the stale client has been corrected.
Whether other sessions need separate review.
variants.next: Document the correlated records and follow the local closure criteria.
variants.pitfall: Treating failed-then-successful authentication as proof of password guessing.

results: The successful session used a password-only path from a device not registered to the user. The session ID matches the alert.
The session accessed a sensitive export screen. The owner’s separately recorded callback denies recognizing this session.
The tenant had routine successes and failures during the day. The aggregate report contains no session identifiers or attribution for this case.
variants.reasoning: Correlated authentication details and the owner’s denial support escalation as suspicious. Visiting an export screen does not establish that data left the system.
remaining: Whether an export completed.
How the credentials or session were obtained.
variants.next: Review the scoped export audit and request authorized incident handling.
variants.pitfall: Calling the account definitely compromised before checking the correlated evidence.

results: The authentication record is present, but its device field is missing and the method field was not retained.
Application logs cannot currently be joined to {{session}}. Owner confirmation has not yet been collected.
The tenant had routine successes and failures during the day. The aggregate report contains no session identifiers or attribution for this case.
variants.reasoning: The available records establish a sequence, not its actor or purpose. Missing correlation prevents a supported disposition.
remaining: The successful session’s authentication method.
Owner recognition and session-linked activity.
variants.next: Request the missing identity record or an analyst handoff with the gaps listed.
variants.pitfall: Interpreting an absent MFA field as proof that MFA was bypassed.

challenge: Write one observation and one hypothesis about this sequence, then choose the lookup that best separates them.
debriefPrinciple: Authenticate the evidence correlation before attributing an authentication event.

title: Repeated MFA prompts and one approval
brief: Assess an MFA approval burst while distinguishing rejected requests from the transaction that created a session.
context: {{user}} reports unexpected authentication notifications at {{org}}. A summary also shows an approved transaction. Your job is to establish whether those records belong to the same activity.

initial.text: Starting at {{time}}, {{count}} authentication prompts were sent to {{user}}.
At {{later}}, one MFA transaction was approved and session {{session}} appears in the sign-in summary.
The initial ticket says “several unexpected prompts”; it does not identify the approved transaction or confirm who initiated it.

unknowns: Which transaction created the session?
What did the user intend to approve?
What happened in the resulting session?
hypotheses: A retrying legitimate application generated multiple prompts.
Repeated prompts induced an unintended approval.
The approved transaction is unrelated to the unexpected prompts.

checks.label: Join prompts to authentication transactions
checks.purpose: Distinguish the approved transaction from surrounding requests.
checks.scope: {{user}} and the transactions associated with {{session}}.

checks.label: Review owner clarification and session use
checks.purpose: Check independently collected user intent against correlated activity.
checks.scope: The case’s owner interview and session {{session}} activity.

checks.label: Read this week’s MFA prompt volume
checks.purpose: Compare general volume without assigning intent to this approval.
checks.scope: Tenant-level aggregate prompt counts only.

results: The approved transaction maps to the user’s managed device; the repeated prompts map to a separate reconnecting application.
The owner clarification identifies the approved transaction as an intended sign-in. Session activity matches the task described in ticket {{ticket}}.
The weekly prompt total is within a broad historical range. It does not establish who initiated or approved this transaction.
variants.reasoning: The transaction join separates the unexpected notifications from the intended sign-in. The corroborated explanation lowers concern for this session.
remaining: Why the application retried prompts.
Whether unrelated rejected attempts require review.
variants.next: Document the transaction mapping and route the retry issue to support.
variants.pitfall: Assigning one approval to every prompt in a nearby time window.

results: The approved transaction maps to an unfamiliar device and is part of the same request sequence as the rejected prompts.
The owner says the approval was made to stop the notifications, not to sign in. The resulting session attempted a new credential registration.
The weekly prompt total is within a broad historical range. It does not establish who initiated or approved this transaction.
variants.reasoning: Transaction correlation and clarified user intent support suspicion of an unintended approval. The credential-registration attempt requires its own outcome check.
remaining: Whether the registration completed.
Whether other active sessions were affected.
variants.next: Read the registration outcome and escalate through the approved response process.
variants.pitfall: Assuming that a valid MFA approval necessarily represents informed user intent.

results: Prompt identifiers were retained, but the approval-to-session join is missing from the export.
The owner remembers approving a prompt but cannot identify it; session telemetry is incomplete.
The weekly prompt total is within a broad historical range. It does not establish who initiated or approved this transaction.
variants.reasoning: A burst and an approval are known, but the missing transaction mapping prevents reliable attribution.
remaining: Which approval created {{session}}.
Whether that approval was intentional.
variants.next: Obtain the original transaction records and retain an unresolved handoff.
variants.pitfall: Converting temporal proximity into a confirmed transaction relationship.

challenge: Which field would you require before stating that the unexpected prompt burst produced this session?
debriefPrinciple: Correlate the exact MFA transaction; a nearby approval is not automatically the same event.

title: Two locations, one short interval
brief: Investigate a location anomaly without treating an IP-derived location as the user’s physical position.
context: An alert at {{org}} flags {{user}} for sign-ins assigned to distant regions. Both entries are successful, but the summary gives little information about network routing or device continuity.

initial.text: A sign-in at {{time}} and another at {{later}} were mapped to distant regions by IP enrichment.
The later sign-in used {{ip}} and is associated with session {{session}}.
The summary contains browser labels but no stable device identifier or approved egress comparison.

unknowns: Does the later source belong to an approved VPN or proxy?
Do stable device and authentication records connect the sessions?
Does the user recognize the later activity?
hypotheses: VPN or proxy routing changed the apparent location.
A different actor established the later session.
The location enrichment or session mapping is inaccurate.

checks.label: Check routing and stable device evidence
checks.purpose: Compare the source with current egress inventory and session device identifiers.
checks.scope: The two sign-ins, {{ip}}, and the current approved-egress inventory.

checks.label: Read the session-linked activity review
checks.purpose: Compare the later session with independently recorded owner recognition.
checks.scope: Session {{session}} and the related owner callback.

checks.label: Read the organization’s office locations
checks.purpose: Understand the footprint without establishing where this user signed in.
checks.scope: Published internal office region list only.

results: Both records share the same stable managed-device identity and authentication binding. {{ip}} is a currently approved VPN egress.
The owner confirms the VPN switch in an independent callback; session actions match the stated work.
The organization operates in several regions. The office directory neither identifies the source network nor links a person to this sign-in.
variants.reasoning: Current routing evidence and device continuity explain the apparent travel. This reduces concern for the location alert while leaving unrelated activity outside scope.
remaining: Whether geolocation enrichment needs correction.
Whether any separate session alerts exist.
variants.next: Record the routing explanation and apply the established review criteria.
variants.pitfall: Treating an IP geolocation label as measured physical travel.

results: The later record has a different device identity. {{ip}} is absent from the current approved-egress inventory, and the session used a newly issued token.
The owner denies the later session. Its activity includes an unexpected download request for a restricted document.
The organization operates in several regions. The office directory neither identifies the source network nor links a person to this sign-in.
variants.reasoning: Different device evidence, owner denial, and unexpected session activity support escalation. An unlisted egress alone would not establish maliciousness.
remaining: Whether the download completed.
How the new token was issued.
variants.next: Correlate token issuance and download outcome in the incident review.
variants.pitfall: Using unfamiliar geography as the sole proof of an attacker.

results: The egress inventory is incomplete for this provider, and the later record has no stable device ID.
The relevant application logs are delayed, and owner confirmation is unavailable.
The organization operates in several regions. The office directory neither identifies the source network nor links a person to this sign-in.
variants.reasoning: The location anomaly cannot currently distinguish routing behavior from a different actor.
remaining: Current egress ownership.
Stable device evidence and session-linked activity.
variants.next: Request the missing routing and device records before assigning a final disposition.
variants.pitfall: Assuming that missing device data means a new device was used.

challenge: Rewrite “the user traveled between these countries” as an observation supported by the alert.
debriefPrinciple: Describe enrichment as enrichment and verify the underlying session and network relationship.

title: A newly consented application
brief: Assess a new application grant by checking the exact application, permissions, authorization, and use.
context: A consent alert at {{org}} shows {{user}} granting an application access. The application’s friendly name resembles an internal utility, but friendly names are not sufficient identifiers.

initial.text: At {{time}}, {{user}} granted an application access to profile information and file metadata.
The application name is new to the alert’s recent-history window.
At {{later}}, a token associated with the new grant was used; the summary omits object-level activity.

unknowns: Does the application ID match an approved integration?
Were the exact permissions approved for this user?
Which resources did the token access?
hypotheses: An approved integration was introduced through a planned rollout.
A misleading application obtained access the user did not intend.
Inventory or audit gaps prevent assessment of a legitimate or abusive grant.

checks.label: Match the application and approved grant
checks.purpose: Compare immutable application identifiers and permission scope with the approval record.
checks.scope: The alerted application ID, grant, and linked approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Review token use and owner clarification
checks.purpose: Read scoped resource accesses and independently recorded user intent.
checks.scope: Tokens issued from the alerted grant during the case window.

checks.label: Read the application’s display-name history
checks.purpose: Look for naming changes without treating the name as proof of identity.
checks.scope: Historical friendly names for the alerted application ID.

results: The immutable application ID and exact permissions match an approved rollout in {{ticket}}. The user is included in that rollout.
Token access is limited to the documented test folder, and the owner confirms enrolling in the rollout.
The displayed application name has been edited before. A friendly-name history does not establish approval, publisher identity, or legitimate token use.
variants.reasoning: Identifier matching, permission approval, and scoped use support a legitimate rollout explanation. Approval alone would not validate all future token activity.
remaining: Whether access remains limited over time.
Whether the rollout’s access expiration is enforced.
variants.next: Record the grant and resource scope for follow-up under the rollout policy.
variants.pitfall: Approving an application based only on its familiar display name.

results: The application ID differs from the approved internal utility despite a similar name. No matching permission approval exists in the current change system.
The owner says the consent screen appeared in an unsolicited document invitation. The token enumerated restricted folder metadata outside the stated task.
The displayed application name has been edited before. A friendly-name history does not establish approval, publisher identity, or legitimate token use.
variants.reasoning: The identifier mismatch and unexpected resource use support suspicion of a misleading consent grant. Metadata enumeration is not proof that file contents were downloaded.
remaining: Whether additional permissions were granted.
Whether file-content access occurred.
variants.next: Escalate the grant for authorized review and correlate subsequent resource operations.
variants.pitfall: Equating an application’s friendly name with a verified integration identity.

results: The application ID is available, but the approval system export lacks the corresponding integration records.
Token-use telemetry stops at authentication, so the accessed resources cannot be determined.
The displayed application name has been edited before. A friendly-name history does not establish approval, publisher identity, or legitimate token use.
variants.reasoning: The grant exists, but approval and actual use remain unverified.
remaining: Whether the exact grant was approved.
Which resources were accessed.
variants.next: Obtain the current approval record and object-level access audit.
variants.pitfall: Treating a missing inventory entry in an incomplete export as proof of unauthorized access.

challenge: Which identifiers and permission fields should your prompt require before comparing this app with an approved one?
debriefPrinciple: Match immutable identity and exact scope, then verify what the grant was used to do.

title: A privileged role was granted
brief: Determine whether a privileged role assignment and its use fit an approved change.
context: A privileged role was assigned to {{user}} at {{org}}. The alert shows the role and time, but the approval, duration, and actions are not included in the first evidence packet.

initial.text: At {{time}}, {{user}} received a role that permits modifying group membership.
At {{later}}, a group membership change was recorded under the same account.
The initial summary does not state whether the grant was eligible, approved, time-limited, or still active.

unknowns: Who approved the exact role and duration?
Which group was changed and for what purpose?
Was the role removed or expired as expected?
hypotheses: A planned administration task used approved temporary privilege.
Privilege was granted or used outside the authorized scope.
The available audit export cannot connect approval, grant, and action.

checks.label: Read grant approval and lifecycle
checks.purpose: Verify the assignment, approver, expiration, and current state.
checks.scope: The alerted assignment for {{user}} and approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Inspect the privileged operation
checks.purpose: Read the changed group and the operation’s relationship to the approved task.
checks.scope: Operations performed during the exact role-assignment interval.

checks.label: Read the account’s historical role count
checks.purpose: Provide history without authorizing the current grant.
checks.scope: Aggregate prior role assignments for {{user}}.

results: A valid approval in {{ticket}} names the exact role, account, and short duration. The assignment expired at the approved time.
The only recorded write added the specified service group to the documented project group; the object IDs match the change plan.
The account has held administrative roles before. Historical privilege does not authorize this assignment or its associated change.
variants.reasoning: The approval, lifecycle, and observed operation align with the planned task. The conclusion applies to the examined audit interval.
remaining: Whether all downstream group effects match the change plan.
Whether the audit interval is complete.
variants.next: Attach the approval and object-level audit to the review record.
variants.pitfall: Treating any privileged role grant as either automatically malicious or automatically justified.

results: The current approval record names a different role and account. The alerted assignment has no expiration.
The account added an unapproved external principal to a sensitive group outside the documented task.
The account has held administrative roles before. Historical privilege does not authorize this assignment or its associated change.
variants.reasoning: The approval mismatch and out-of-scope privileged operation support escalation. The initiating actor still requires investigation.
remaining: Who initiated the assignment.
Whether the external principal used the new access.
variants.next: Review assignment provenance and subsequent access through the authorized response workflow.
variants.pitfall: Checking only that some change ticket exists instead of matching its exact scope.

results: The assignment record is intact, but the linked approval has not been retained in the available export.
The group operation is recorded without the target object identifier, preventing comparison with the planned task.
The account has held administrative roles before. Historical privilege does not authorize this assignment or its associated change.
variants.reasoning: The grant and a write occurred, but missing approval and target details prevent a defensible authorization assessment.
remaining: Exact approval scope.
Target group and membership delta.
variants.next: Retrieve the original approval and object-level directory event.
variants.pitfall: Assuming that an account name alone proves an operation matched an approved task.

challenge: What would your verifier compare besides the existence of a change ticket?
debriefPrinciple: Authorization is a match between identity, action, resource, and time—not just a ticket number.

title: Recovery changes before a password reset
brief: Assess a recovery-factor change followed by a password reset without inferring the actor from the audit username.
context: The recovery workflow for {{user}} at {{org}} changed shortly before a password reset. The summary identifies the affected account but omits the verification path and initiating support session.

initial.text: At {{time}}, a recovery contact for {{user}} was changed.
At {{later}}, the password-reset workflow completed for the same account.
A later sign-in is linked to session {{session}}; verification steps and helpdesk correlation are absent from the alert.

unknowns: Which verification path authorized the contact change?
Does a legitimate helpdesk case match the exact actions?
Does the user recognize the recovery changes and new session?
hypotheses: An approved recovery case replaced an inaccessible contact.
The recovery process was abused to gain access.
Incomplete workflow records obscure the legitimacy of the sequence.

checks.label: Read recovery verification records
checks.purpose: Check the verified identity path and exact helpdesk action scope.
checks.scope: The contact change, reset transaction, and related case {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Read owner confirmation and resulting access
checks.purpose: Correlate independent owner clarification and the subsequent session.
checks.scope: Session {{session}} and the recovery case’s callback record.

checks.label: Read monthly password-reset volume
checks.purpose: Provide operational context without validating this reset.
checks.scope: Monthly reset counts for {{org}} only.

results: The original workflow shows the required identity verification and an approved contact replacement in {{ticket}}. The transaction IDs match the alert.
The account owner confirms the replacement through the recorded verification channel. The later session uses the registered managed device and expected application.
Password resets are common in the organization. The monthly total contains no evidence about verification of this recovery transaction.
variants.reasoning: Matched workflow verification and owner confirmation support an authorized recovery explanation. Subsequent access remains separately reviewable.
remaining: Whether obsolete recovery contacts were removed.
Whether all reset-related sessions are accounted for.
variants.next: Document the transaction IDs and complete the recovery review.
variants.pitfall: Using the affected account’s name as proof that the account owner initiated the reset.

results: The verification step is explicitly recorded as skipped by an administrative override, and the helpdesk approval does not authorize a contact change.
The owner denies requesting recovery. The new session registered another authentication method from an unfamiliar device.
Password resets are common in the organization. The monthly total contains no evidence about verification of this recovery transaction.
variants.reasoning: The recorded override, approval mismatch, and denied activity support escalation for recovery-process abuse. The responsible actor is not yet established.
remaining: Who authorized or used the override.
Whether the additional authentication method remains active.
variants.next: Correlate the administrative session and request authorized containment review.
variants.pitfall: Interpreting a completed recovery workflow as evidence that identity verification succeeded.

results: The available workflow export records completion but omits the verification decisions and operator session.
Owner confirmation is pending, and the device record for {{session}} has not arrived.
Password resets are common in the organization. The monthly total contains no evidence about verification of this recovery transaction.
variants.reasoning: Completion is established, but authorization and actor attribution are unresolved.
remaining: Verification decisions and operator identity.
Owner recognition of the resulting session.
variants.next: Obtain the original recovery workflow and independent owner confirmation.
variants.pitfall: Treating a missing verification field as an explicit verification failure.

challenge: How would you distinguish “verification skipped” from “verification record unavailable” in the output schema?
debriefPrinciple: Separate workflow completion, verification outcome, and actor attribution.

title: A new external forwarding rule
brief: Assess a forwarding rule by checking its creator, destination, approval, and actual message matches.
context: A mailbox rule for {{user}} at {{org}} forwards matching messages outside the organization. The summary shows a rule change but not whether it matched messages or was approved.

initial.text: At {{time}}, a forwarding rule targeting an address at {{domain}} was created for {{user}}.
The rule applies to a subset of incoming messages; the alert omits its full condition and creator session.
At {{later}}, the mailbox received new messages, but the initial packet contains no rule-match or delivery outcomes.

unknowns: Who or what created the rule?
Was this exact destination and condition approved?
Did any messages match and reach the destination?
hypotheses: An approved workflow routes selected messages to a service provider.
An unauthorized rule redirects information.
A rule exists but the available audit cannot establish intent or effect.

checks.label: Read the rule and approval context
checks.purpose: Match rule conditions, creator session, and destination to approved scope.
checks.scope: The alerted rule for {{user}} and the related approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Trace matched messages and delivery outcomes
checks.purpose: Establish actual rule effects rather than inferring delivery from configuration.
checks.scope: Messages matched by the alerted rule during the case window.

checks.label: Read the external domain’s public description
checks.purpose: Provide context without proving who controls the mailbox or authorizing forwarding.
checks.scope: Cached descriptive record for {{domain}} only.

results: The creator session belongs to the approved administrator, and the exact destination and invoice-only condition match {{ticket}}.
The trace contains only the approved test message and its expected delivery receipt. No other matching deliveries appear in the examined window.
A descriptive domain record labels the destination as a communications service. It does not verify the receiving account or authorize forwarding.
variants.reasoning: The exact rule scope and observed test delivery align with the approved workflow. This does not guarantee that future rule matches will remain appropriate.
remaining: Whether the rule expires as planned.
Whether the destination account’s access remains restricted.
variants.next: Record the scope and schedule the policy-defined follow-up.
variants.pitfall: Assuming that an approved provider domain authorizes any forwarding address on that domain.

results: The rule was created by an unrecognized session. Its condition includes sensitive project messages, and no matching destination approval exists.
Message tracing confirms delivery of matching project messages to the configured external address.
A descriptive domain record labels the destination as a communications service. It does not verify the receiving account or authorize forwarding.
variants.reasoning: Unapproved scope and confirmed delivery support escalation for unauthorized forwarding. The evidence establishes delivery, not what the recipient later did with the messages.
remaining: The creator session’s origin.
The full set of affected messages.
variants.next: Preserve scoped delivery records and request authorized incident handling.
variants.pitfall: Calling exfiltration complete from rule creation alone without delivery evidence.

results: The rule conditions are available, but the creator session and approval record are missing from the export.
The trace records rule evaluation but not final delivery outcomes.
A descriptive domain record labels the destination as a communications service. It does not verify the receiving account or authorize forwarding.
variants.reasoning: A potentially consequential configuration exists, but authorization and actual delivery remain unresolved.
remaining: Who created the rule and with what authority.
Whether matched messages were delivered.
variants.next: Retrieve the creator audit and complete message trace.
variants.pitfall: Equating a forwarding configuration with a proven transfer.

challenge: Write separate findings for configuration risk and observed delivery.
debriefPrinciple: Configuration, execution, and delivery are distinct evidence stages.

title: An invoice attachment was opened
brief: Assess an attachment alert by correlating the exact file, analysis results, and endpoint behavior.
context: {{user}} opened an invoice attachment received at {{org}}. The mail gateway assigns it an unusual-file warning, while the initial endpoint summary only confirms that a viewer opened the file.

initial.text: At {{time}}, an invoice-themed message from an address at {{domain}} delivered an attachment to {{user}}.
The attachment hash is recorded, and the gateway flags a file-type mismatch for review.
At {{later}}, {{host}} opened the attachment in a document viewer; the summary does not include child processes or file-analysis detail.

unknowns: Do analysis results refer to the exact attachment hash?
What did the endpoint do after opening the file?
Is the sender relationship independently verified?
hypotheses: A legitimate supplier export uses an unusual container or extension.
The attachment attempted activity outside document viewing.
File-analysis or endpoint gaps prevent disposition.

checks.label: Read exact-hash attachment analysis
checks.purpose: Examine the actual file structure and analysis for this attachment.
checks.scope: The hash recorded in the alerted message only.

checks.label: Read the post-open process timeline
checks.purpose: Correlate the viewer with subsequent processes and an existing supplier-verification note.
checks.scope: {{host}}, the attachment-open event, and its immediate process tree.

checks.label: Read the sender’s display-name history
checks.purpose: Understand prior presentation without authenticating this message.
checks.scope: Historical displayed names for the sender address only.

results: Analysis of the exact hash identifies a supplier-generated archive containing static invoice data; the warning concerns its extension. No active content appears in the supplied analysis.
The endpoint timeline shows only the expected viewer and temporary rendering files. An independently recorded supplier callback confirms this invoice transfer.
The sender has previously used an invoice-related display name. Display names do not authenticate the message or establish attachment safety.
variants.reasoning: Exact-file analysis, correlated viewing behavior, and supplier confirmation support lower concern for the examined event. Analysis has finite coverage.
remaining: Whether any other attachment version was received.
Whether endpoint telemetry covers the full relevant interval.
variants.next: Record the exact hash and the documented explanation for the warning.
variants.pitfall: Calling a file safe solely because a scan returned no detection.

results: Analysis of the exact hash identifies active content inconsistent with a static invoice and records an attempted external resource request.
The viewer started an unexpected scripting process, which attempted a connection unrelated to the supplier workflow.
The sender has previously used an invoice-related display name. Display names do not authenticate the message or establish attachment safety.
variants.reasoning: File analysis and correlated endpoint behavior support suspicion of an attachment-driven execution attempt. The records do not establish every attempted action succeeded.
remaining: Whether the network request completed.
What changes the spawned process made.
variants.next: Review the scoped execution and network outcomes under incident procedure.
variants.pitfall: Treating an attempted connection as a confirmed data transfer.

results: The available analysis result refers to a different attachment hash; the alerted hash has no completed analysis.
The endpoint has a telemetry gap immediately after the viewer opened the file.
The sender has previously used an invoice-related display name. Display names do not authenticate the message or establish attachment safety.
variants.reasoning: The file was opened, but neither a matching analysis nor a complete behavior trace is available.
remaining: Analysis of the exact delivered hash.
The missing post-open process and network records.
variants.next: Obtain exact-hash analysis and endpoint records before classifying the event.
variants.pitfall: Applying a clean result for a different file to the alerted attachment.

challenge: What identifiers must match before you use a sandbox or scanner result as evidence?
debriefPrinciple: Verification applies to the exact artifact and observed behavior, not a similar filename.

title: A payment change inside an existing thread
brief: Evaluate a changed payment instruction using message provenance and independently verified business intent.
context: A reply in an ongoing supplier conversation asks {{user}} at {{org}} to change payment details. The quoted thread looks familiar, but the initial packet does not establish the origin of the new instruction.

initial.text: At {{time}}, {{user}} received a reply containing a new payment destination instruction.
The message includes quoted text from a previous conversation and an external reply address at {{domain}}.
At {{later}}, the proposed change is pending review; no completed payment is recorded in the case packet.

unknowns: Does the new message belong to the verified sender account?
Were payment details confirmed through an independent channel?
Has any workflow action already occurred?
hypotheses: A legitimate supplier requested a verified payment-detail change.
A spoofed or compromised conversation introduced an unauthorized change.
Message provenance and business confirmation remain incomplete.

checks.label: Read the message provenance comparison
checks.purpose: Compare exact sender, reply route, and message identifiers with the known conversation.
checks.scope: The new message and the known-good conversation records.

checks.label: Read independent verification and workflow status
checks.purpose: Check a callback using pre-existing contact details and the current change state.
checks.scope: The case’s verification record and pending change request only.

checks.label: Read the supplier’s public business profile
checks.purpose: Provide background without validating this instruction.
checks.scope: Cached public description of the named supplier.

results: The new message’s sender and reply route match the established account identifiers; the conversation linkage is intact.
A callback using the previously stored supplier number confirms the requested details. The change remains within the approval workflow and no payment has yet been made.
The public profile describes a real business relationship. It does not authenticate the message or authorize new payment details.
variants.reasoning: Message consistency and independent business verification support a legitimate change request. Financial execution still requires the normal approval process.
remaining: Whether the required financial approvals are complete.
Whether the final entered details match the verified record.
variants.next: Document verification and leave the decision to the established approval workflow.
variants.pitfall: Allowing the email itself to authorize a payment change.

results: The reply route differs from the established account and uses a similar-looking address; quoted text was copied into a new message chain.
The supplier denies the change during a callback to the pre-existing contact. The change request is still pending.
The public profile describes a real business relationship. It does not authenticate the message or authorize new payment details.
variants.reasoning: Provenance mismatch and independent denial support suspicion of a fraudulent instruction. The current evidence shows an attempt, not a completed payment loss.
remaining: How the prior thread text was obtained.
Whether other recipients received the same request.
variants.next: Preserve the message and escalate the attempted change through the existing process.
variants.pitfall: Treating familiar quoted text as proof that the new instruction is authentic.

results: The exported message lacks the full routing fields needed to compare it with the established sender.
Independent supplier confirmation is pending; the payment-change request has not been approved.
The public profile describes a real business relationship. It does not authenticate the message or authorize new payment details.
variants.reasoning: The requested change cannot currently be authenticated. The pending workflow state should be kept explicit.
remaining: Complete message provenance.
Independent confirmation through an established contact.
variants.next: Request the original message and independent verification before disposition.
variants.pitfall: Guessing authenticity from writing style or a familiar signature.

challenge: What would count as independent confirmation, rather than another claim from the same email?
debriefPrinciple: Verify business intent through a channel independent of the disputed instruction.

title: A new external collaboration link
brief: Assess an external sharing change by examining exact access scope and actual use.
context: {{org}} receives a sharing alert for a project document owned by {{user}}. A link was created for an external destination, but the summary omits its audience restrictions and whether anyone used it.

initial.text: At {{time}}, {{user}} created a sharing link for a project document.
The destination includes a contact at {{domain}}. The initial record does not state whether the link is recipient-bound or broadly accessible.
At {{later}}, the document has an access event whose principal and outcome are omitted from the summary.

unknowns: What exact audience and capabilities does the link grant?
Does the recipient and document scope match an approved collaboration?
Who actually accessed the document?
hypotheses: A restricted link supports an approved collaboration.
An overly broad or unauthorized share exposed sensitive material.
Incomplete permission or access records prevent assessment.

checks.label: Read effective sharing permissions
checks.purpose: Inspect audience, recipient binding, expiration, and approved resource scope.
checks.scope: The alerted document, link ID, and approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Read principal-level access outcomes
checks.purpose: Identify the principal and actual view or download outcome.
checks.scope: Accesses using the alerted sharing link during the case window.

checks.label: Read the project’s collaboration count
checks.purpose: Provide volume context without validating this link.
checks.scope: Aggregate sharing counts for this project only.

results: The link is bound to the approved recipient, allows viewing only, and expires within the period in {{ticket}}. The document ID matches the approved scope.
The only recorded access is a successful view by that verified recipient. No download is recorded in the inspected interval.
The project has several external collaborations. That history does not establish the permissions or authorization of this link.
variants.reasoning: Effective permissions and the observed principal match the approved collaboration. The limited audit interval does not prove all future access will remain appropriate.
remaining: Whether the link expires as configured.
Whether the document’s sensitivity changes during the collaboration.
variants.next: Record effective permissions and the policy-defined expiration review.
variants.pitfall: Assuming an external share is automatically public.

results: The link permits anonymous downloading and covers a sensitive document not included in the current approval.
The access audit records a successful download using the anonymous link; no named recipient can be attributed to that event.
The project has several external collaborations. That history does not establish the permissions or authorization of this link.
variants.reasoning: Broad unauthorized scope and a completed download support escalation. The anonymous log does not identify the human downloader.
remaining: Who obtained the link.
Whether additional documents were exposed.
variants.next: Preserve the effective-permission and download records for authorized incident response.
variants.pitfall: Assigning anonymous access to the intended recipient without evidence.

results: The audit export shows link creation but omits its effective audience and capability settings.
The access summary cannot be resolved to a principal or a final outcome.
The project has several external collaborations. That history does not establish the permissions or authorization of this link.
variants.reasoning: A sharing change and a later access event exist, but exposure and actual use cannot yet be established.
remaining: Effective permissions at the event time.
The access principal and outcome.
variants.next: Retrieve the historical permission snapshot and full access event.
variants.pitfall: Treating a generic access event as a successful external download.

challenge: Separate the questions “who could access it?” and “who did access it?” in your output.
debriefPrinciple: Effective access scope and observed access are different security claims.

title: A burst of mailbox reads
brief: Assess a mailbox-read burst by identifying the principal, authorized purpose, and exact operations.
context: Monitoring at {{org}} reports a burst of API reads associated with {{user}}. The alert groups several operations together and does not distinguish metadata listing from message-content retrieval.

initial.text: At {{time}}, {{count}} mailbox API operations occurred for {{user}} in a short interval.
The client label differs from the account’s recent interactive mail sessions.
Operations continue until {{later}}, but the summary lacks application ID, grant scope, and per-operation result.

unknowns: Which application or session performed the operations?
Was the exact mailbox access scope approved?
Were operations metadata reads, content reads, or failures?
hypotheses: An approved export or indexing task accessed the mailbox.
An unauthorized principal collected mailbox information.
Grouped or incomplete audit records exaggerate or obscure the activity.

checks.label: Read the application grant and job approval
checks.purpose: Match immutable client identity, delegated scope, and approved purpose.
checks.scope: The alerted client, mailbox {{user}}, and job approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Read operation-level mailbox results
checks.purpose: Separate metadata, message-content reads, and failed operations.
checks.scope: The alerted operation IDs during the case window.

checks.label: Read the mailbox’s message count
checks.purpose: Understand mailbox size without validating any read.
checks.scope: Aggregate message count only; no message content.

results: The client ID and mailbox scope match an approved indexing job in {{ticket}}. The job identity has the documented restricted grant.
Operation-level audit shows metadata listing only for the approved folder set; the job completed at the expected time.
The mailbox contains many messages. Its size cannot identify the requesting application or establish whether the observed reads were authorized.
variants.reasoning: The matched job identity and restricted operation results support a legitimate indexing explanation. This assessment does not authorize broader message-content access.
remaining: Whether the grant is removed after the job.
Whether later operations remain within scope.
variants.next: Document client identity and operation types in the review.
variants.pitfall: Calling every mailbox API operation a full-message download.

results: The client ID has no matching job approval and uses a grant broader than the recorded business task.
The audit confirms successful message-body and attachment reads from folders outside the stated task.
The mailbox contains many messages. Its size cannot identify the requesting application or establish whether the observed reads were authorized.
variants.reasoning: Unapproved client scope and confirmed content retrieval support escalation. The evidence does not by itself establish where retrieved data was later stored.
remaining: How the application obtained its grant.
Whether other mailboxes were accessed.
variants.next: Review grant provenance and the bounded set of affected mailboxes.
variants.pitfall: Equating API access with confirmed downstream disclosure without tracing the next stage.

results: The audit export resolves the user but not the application principal or grant ID.
The grouped counter cannot distinguish successful content reads from metadata requests and retries.
The mailbox contains many messages. Its size cannot identify the requesting application or establish whether the observed reads were authorized.
variants.reasoning: The activity volume is known, but identity, authorization, and read type remain unresolved.
remaining: Application principal and grant scope.
Per-operation type and success outcome.
variants.next: Obtain principal-resolved operation logs before labeling the burst.
variants.pitfall: Treating an aggregate request count as a count of successfully retrieved messages.

challenge: What operation fields would you require before reporting that message contents were accessed?
debriefPrinciple: Counts need operation semantics, identity, and outcomes to become meaningful evidence.

title: A collaboration invite with a familiar logo
brief: Evaluate a collaboration invitation using link destination, tenant identity, and observed user interaction.
context: {{user}} at {{org}} reports a document invitation that uses a familiar service name and logo. The email link was followed, but the initial packet does not show whether credentials were entered or a session was issued.

initial.text: At {{time}}, an invitation from an address at {{domain}} asked {{user}} to open a shared document.
At {{later}}, {{host}} followed the invitation link and displayed a sign-in page.
The report says “the page looked familiar.” It does not identify the final origin, tenant, or submitted form outcome.

unknowns: What final origin and tenant did the redirect chain reach?
Does the invitation match an approved collaboration?
Were credentials submitted or a session created?
hypotheses: A legitimate external collaboration redirected to an approved sign-in service.
A lookalike sign-in page attempted to collect authentication information.
Available telemetry cannot establish the destination or interaction outcome.

checks.label: Read the exact redirect and invitation context
checks.purpose: Compare the final origin and tenant with the approved collaboration record.
checks.scope: The reported message’s link chain and approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Read the browser interaction and session outcome
checks.purpose: Distinguish viewing a page, submitting a form, and obtaining a session.
checks.scope: {{host}} and related identity events in the case window; no password values.

checks.label: Read the service’s public branding description
checks.purpose: Provide context while recognizing that branding can be copied.
checks.scope: A cached public description of the claimed service.

results: The redirect ends at the approved identity origin and the verified partner tenant named in {{ticket}}. The invitation document ID matches that collaboration.
The user completed the expected sign-in flow, and the resulting session opened only the approved document in the inspected interval.
The claimed service uses the logo and wording shown in the message. Branding alone does not verify the destination origin or tenant.
variants.reasoning: Exact destination and tenant matching plus the expected session outcome support the approved-collaboration explanation. A familiar logo alone would not.
remaining: Whether the document’s permission scope remains appropriate.
Whether any other invitation links were followed.
variants.next: Record the final origin, tenant, and document identifiers.
variants.pitfall: Authenticating an invitation by appearance instead of exact destination and context.

results: The redirect ends at a different origin that imitates the service’s sign-in page. No matching collaboration invitation exists in the approved record.
The browser trace records a form submission to that different origin; no corresponding session was issued by the legitimate identity service.
The claimed service uses the logo and wording shown in the message. Branding alone does not verify the destination origin or tenant.
variants.reasoning: Destination mismatch and submission to the imitating origin support escalation for a credential-collection attempt. The trace deliberately excludes the submitted secret values.
remaining: Whether submitted credentials were later used.
Whether any related sessions or recovery changes occurred.
variants.next: Review subsequent identity events and request authorized account-response handling.
variants.pitfall: Claiming account takeover solely because the user visited a sign-in page.

results: The proxy log retains the first link but not the final redirect origin, and the collaboration record is unavailable.
Interaction telemetry confirms page viewing but does not retain a form-submission outcome.
The claimed service uses the logo and wording shown in the message. Branding alone does not verify the destination origin or tenant.
variants.reasoning: The page was visited, but destination identity and possible credential submission remain unresolved.
remaining: Final redirect origin and tenant.
Whether a form was submitted and a session issued.
variants.next: Obtain the missing redirect and identity outcomes without collecting password contents.
variants.pitfall: Treating page display as proof that the user submitted credentials.

challenge: List the separate evidence needed to support “visited,” “submitted,” and “authenticated.”
debriefPrinciple: Branding, destination identity, and user interaction outcome must be evaluated separately.

title: An object store changed its access policy
brief: Assess a storage-access change by testing effective permissions and examining access outcomes.
context: A cloud control-plane alert at {{org}} reports an access-policy change to a project object store. The summary contains a permission statement but does not account for every applicable restriction or the objects involved.

initial.text: At {{time}}, a policy on a project object store was changed.
A statement mentioning a broad audience appears in the new policy; the initial summary omits conditions and organization-level restrictions.
At {{later}}, requests to the store increased, but their principals, requested objects, and outcomes are not included.

unknowns: What access is effective after all relevant conditions and controls?
Which objects and approval scope are involved?
Did any external request succeed?
hypotheses: A planned change exposes only approved public objects under enforced restrictions.
The change permits unapproved access to sensitive objects.
Incomplete policy or access evidence prevents a reliable exposure assessment.

checks.label: Read effective policy and approved scope
checks.purpose: Evaluate the complete permission state for the affected objects.
checks.scope: The affected store, applicable restrictions, and approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Read principal-level object access outcomes
checks.purpose: Distinguish requests, denials, and successful object retrievals.
checks.scope: Requests to affected objects during the case window.

checks.label: Read the store’s total object count
checks.purpose: Provide size context without determining exposure.
checks.scope: Object totals and aggregate size only.

results: The complete policy restricts the broad-audience statement to a public documentation prefix approved in {{ticket}}. Private prefixes remain denied under the evaluated controls.
Access logs show successful reads only for the approved public documentation; sampled requests for private objects were denied.
The store contains many objects of mixed purposes. Aggregate object count does not establish effective permission or successful access to any particular object.
variants.reasoning: Effective scope and recorded access match the intended publication. This conclusion covers the examined policy and objects, not every future configuration.
remaining: Whether later policy changes broaden the scope.
Whether object classification remains correct.
variants.next: Document the evaluated scope and policy version.
variants.pitfall: Reading one broad-looking policy line without evaluating its conditions and other controls.

results: The effective policy permits unauthenticated reads of a sensitive project prefix, outside the current approval.
Data-plane audit confirms successful external retrieval of objects from that sensitive prefix.
The store contains many objects of mixed purposes. Aggregate object count does not establish effective permission or successful access to any particular object.
variants.reasoning: Unapproved effective access and successful sensitive-object reads support escalation. The logs do not establish the identity or later actions of an unauthenticated recipient.
remaining: Which object versions were retrieved.
How the policy change was initiated.
variants.next: Preserve the policy version and scoped object-access events for response review.
variants.pitfall: Claiming data disclosure from a risky policy alone without checking access outcomes.

results: The policy export omits a referenced access-control condition, so effective access cannot be computed from this packet.
Access records show request counts but omit outcome and object identifiers.
The store contains many objects of mixed purposes. Aggregate object count does not establish effective permission or successful access to any particular object.
variants.reasoning: A policy change and traffic increase occurred, but neither effective exposure nor successful retrieval is established.
remaining: Complete policy conditions and restrictions.
Object-specific request outcomes.
variants.next: Obtain the missing policy and data-plane records.
variants.pitfall: Treating an increase in requests as proof that protected objects were downloaded.

challenge: What belongs in separate “possible exposure” and “observed access” findings?
debriefPrinciple: Evaluate complete permissions and distinguish exposure capability from actual access.

title: A service identity received broader permissions
brief: Assess an expanded service-identity policy by comparing approved scope with effective privileges and subsequent use.
context: A service identity used by {{org}} received a revised policy. The diff adds actions and resources, but the initial alert does not show why the change was made or whether those privileges were exercised.

initial.text: At {{time}}, the policy for a project service identity was revised to include additional actions.
The new version references more resources than the preceding version; approval scope is not attached.
At {{later}}, that identity made API requests, but the summary omits the exact actions and outcomes.

unknowns: Which privileges are effective under the full policy?
Does the exact expansion match approved work?
Were newly permitted actions used and with what outcomes?
hypotheses: A planned service deployment requires the narrowly approved expansion.
An unauthorized policy expansion enabled out-of-scope actions.
Missing policy or activity records obscure the change’s significance.

checks.label: Compare effective scope with approval
checks.purpose: Read the policy version, resource conditions, and exact approved change.
checks.scope: The alerted identity, both policy versions, and {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Review newly permitted API operations
checks.purpose: Check how the added privileges were actually used.
checks.scope: Calls by the affected identity after the policy change.

checks.label: Read the identity’s historical request total
checks.purpose: Provide volume context without validating new privileges.
checks.scope: Aggregate request totals for this service identity.

results: The effective additions are restricted to the deployment’s test resources and match the actions and duration in {{ticket}}.
Recorded calls use only the newly approved test-resource actions, and the temporary policy version was reverted at the expected time.
The identity is routinely active. Historical request volume does not authorize added actions or describe the current calls.
variants.reasoning: Exact scope, observed use, and reversion match the approved deployment. This is a bounded assessment of the recorded change.
remaining: Whether all deployment resources are covered by the review.
Whether any later policy revision exists.
variants.next: Attach the policy version and scoped API evidence to the change review.
variants.pitfall: Assuming a larger policy diff always creates unrestricted access.

results: The effective additions permit credential-management actions on production resources beyond the deployment approval.
Audit records confirm the identity used a newly added action to create another credential outside the approved resource set.
The identity is routinely active. Historical request volume does not authorize added actions or describe the current calls.
variants.reasoning: The authorization mismatch and successful out-of-scope credential operation support escalation. Use of the new credential requires separate investigation.
remaining: Who submitted the policy revision.
Whether the newly created credential was used.
variants.next: Correlate the policy-changing session and the new credential’s activity.
variants.pitfall: Treating authorization to deploy one service as approval for all policy additions.

results: The referenced resource-condition document is missing, and the current approval export is incomplete.
API summaries cannot be resolved to individual actions or outcomes for this identity.
The identity is routinely active. Historical request volume does not authorize added actions or describe the current calls.
variants.reasoning: The policy changed, but its effective breadth and practical use are unresolved.
remaining: Complete effective permission inputs.
Action-level requests and results.
variants.next: Retrieve complete policy inputs and identity-resolved API logs.
variants.pitfall: Inferring effective permissions from a partial policy diff.

challenge: Which exact fields must match between a policy change and its approval?
debriefPrinciple: Review effective action and resource scope, then verify the privileges actually exercised.

title: A new programmatic credential appeared
brief: Assess a newly created access credential by correlating its creator, intended rotation, and usage.
context: A new credential was created for a service identity at {{org}}. A nearby activity burst could represent a routine rotation or another actor, and the alert does not include credential-specific attribution.

initial.text: At {{time}}, a new programmatic credential was created for a project service identity.
An older credential is present in the same identity inventory; its retirement status is omitted.
At {{later}}, requests appear from {{ip}}, but the summary does not identify which credential signed them.

unknowns: Was the exact credential creation part of an approved rotation?
Which credential signed the later requests?
Was the old credential retired and the new one used within scope?
hypotheses: An approved rotation replaced an expiring credential.
An unapproved credential was created to maintain access.
Lifecycle and request attribution are insufficient to distinguish the cases.

checks.label: Read credential creation and rotation context
checks.purpose: Verify creator, approval, and lifecycle events without exposing secret material.
checks.scope: Credential identifiers, creator session, and rotation approval {{ticket}}; no secret values.

checks.label: Read credential-attributed API calls
checks.purpose: Identify the requests made using the new credential and their outcomes.
checks.scope: Calls signed by the new credential during the case window.

checks.label: Read the service’s monthly call volume
checks.purpose: Provide general usage context without identifying credential use.
checks.scope: Aggregate service-call count only.

results: The creator session and credential ID match the approved rotation in {{ticket}}. The old credential was disabled after a short documented overlap.
The new credential signs only the expected service calls from the approved runner, with resource scope matching the rotation plan.
The service makes regular monthly calls. Aggregate traffic cannot identify which credential was used or establish approval for its creation.
variants.reasoning: Creation, lifecycle, and credential-attributed use align with the planned rotation. Continued monitoring remains scoped to the service policy.
remaining: Whether the retired credential has any later attempts.
Whether the new credential’s expiry matches the plan.
variants.next: Record the credential IDs and rotation outcomes without copying secret values.
variants.pitfall: Mistaking a documented overlap during rotation for proof of persistence.

results: The credential was created by an unfamiliar administrative session with no matching rotation approval. The old credential remains active.
The new credential successfully listed secrets metadata and attempted calls outside the service’s approved resources.
The service makes regular monthly calls. Aggregate traffic cannot identify which credential was used or establish approval for its creation.
variants.reasoning: Unapproved creation and unexpected credential-attributed use support escalation. Listing metadata does not establish that secret values were retrieved.
remaining: Whether secret-value retrieval succeeded.
The creator session’s provenance.
variants.next: Review the bounded secret-access outcomes and administrative session.
variants.pitfall: Using service-level traffic to attribute activity to a particular credential.

results: The creation event exists, but its initiating session is missing and the rotation record cannot be retrieved.
The available request logs lack the credential identifier needed for attribution.
The service makes regular monthly calls. Aggregate traffic cannot identify which credential was used or establish approval for its creation.
variants.reasoning: Credential creation is established, but approval and subsequent usage cannot be determined from the packet.
remaining: Creator session and exact rotation scope.
Credential-resolved API records.
variants.next: Request credential metadata and attributable API logs, without requesting secret values.
variants.pitfall: Treating a nearby request burst as proof that the new credential made those calls.

challenge: How can you investigate credential use without ever placing the credential’s secret value in the prompt?
debriefPrinciple: Use credential identifiers and audit provenance; secret values are unnecessary for attribution.

title: A sudden burst of cloud resource creation
brief: Assess a provisioning burst using approved workload scope, initiating identity, and observed resource behavior.
context: At {{org}}, cloud monitoring reports a sharp increase in new compute resources. The initial alert emphasizes count and cost estimate but does not establish the workload or creator’s authorization.

initial.text: At {{time}}, {{count}} compute resources were requested under one project identity.
Several resources use a size not common in that project’s recent history.
By {{later}}, some resources are running. The packet omits job labels, creation-session attribution, and network or workload detail.

unknowns: Does an approved workload specify this resource count, size, and duration?
Which session or automation initiated the requests?
What work is actually running on the created resources?
hypotheses: A planned batch or performance test provisioned temporary resources.
An unauthorized workload consumed project capacity.
Inventory and runtime gaps prevent attributing the spike.

checks.label: Read the provisioning identity and job plan
checks.purpose: Match resource scope and creator session to the approved workload.
checks.scope: The alerted request set and job approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Read scoped workload and teardown records
checks.purpose: Inspect the running job identity and lifecycle outcomes.
checks.scope: Only the resources created by the alerted request set.

checks.label: Read the project’s monthly spend trend
checks.purpose: Provide business context without identifying this workload.
checks.scope: Aggregate historical project spend; no billing changes.

results: The request set, machine sizes, and initiating automation identity match the approved load test in {{ticket}}.
The resources run the signed test image, report the expected test job ID, and terminate within the planned interval.
Monthly spend has fluctuated before. A cost trend cannot identify the current workload or establish that it was authorized.
variants.reasoning: Creator, resource scope, and observed workload align with an approved temporary test. High resource count alone was not sufficient for an incident finding.
remaining: Whether every created resource was terminated.
Whether any later requests fall outside the test window.
variants.next: Document the request-to-job mapping and verify the complete teardown list.
variants.pitfall: Treating cost or size anomalies alone as proof of illicit compute use.

results: The initiating credential has no matching workload approval, and the requested sizes exceed the project’s authorized job profile.
Runtime audit shows an unapproved image and sustained outbound connections unrelated to the documented service. Teardown did not occur.
Monthly spend has fluctuated before. A cost trend cannot identify the current workload or establish that it was authorized.
variants.reasoning: Authorization mismatch and unexpected runtime behavior support escalation for an unauthorized workload. A specific purpose, such as mining, is not established by these facts alone.
remaining: What the unapproved image actually executes.
Whether the credential was used in other projects.
variants.next: Request scoped image analysis and credential-use correlation through incident review.
variants.pitfall: Naming a specific malicious workload from resource size or cost alone.

results: The creator identity resolves to a shared automation account, but its job invocation records are unavailable.
Runtime labels are missing and workload telemetry has not arrived.
Monthly spend has fluctuated before. A cost trend cannot identify the current workload or establish that it was authorized.
variants.reasoning: The resource increase is real, but the initiating job and actual workload remain unresolved.
remaining: The originating automation job.
Runtime image and task evidence.
variants.next: Retrieve invocation and workload records before assigning a purpose.
variants.pitfall: Conflating resource provisioning with evidence of what later ran.

challenge: Rewrite the alert as observed capacity changes without guessing the workload’s purpose.
debriefPrinciple: Provisioning volume, workload purpose, and authorization require different evidence.

title: A build job read a deployment secret
brief: Assess a secret read by correlating immutable build inputs, approval, and the destination of the resulting deployment.
context: A CI job at {{org}} read a deployment secret. Secret access can be required for delivery, but the first alert does not show the job’s source revision, approval, or what it deployed.

initial.text: At {{time}}, a CI workload identity successfully read a deployment secret version.
The associated job ran for a change involving {{host}}, but its immutable revision and trust context are absent from the summary.
At {{later}}, the job reports a completed step; the packet does not identify the target environment or artifact digest.

unknowns: Which source revision and workflow definition were executed?
Was that workload identity authorized to read this secret version?
What target and artifact resulted from the job?
hypotheses: An approved deployment used its narrowly scoped secret.
An untrusted or modified build accessed a secret outside its intended context.
Incomplete build provenance prevents assessment of the read.

checks.label: Read immutable build provenance and approval
checks.purpose: Match workflow, revision, identity binding, and secret scope to the approved deployment.
checks.scope: The job, workload identity, secret metadata, and approval {{ticket}}; no secret values.

checks.label: Read deployment and egress outcomes
checks.purpose: Correlate job outputs with the approved target and network destinations.
checks.scope: The alerted job’s artifact, deployment result, and scoped egress metadata.

checks.label: Read pipeline success-rate history
checks.purpose: Understand reliability without validating this run’s provenance.
checks.scope: Aggregate success and failure counts only.

results: Immutable provenance identifies the reviewed revision and protected workflow in {{ticket}}. The workload identity is bound to that workflow and the required secret version.
The resulting artifact digest and deployment target match the approved release, and recorded egress is limited to the expected services.
The pipeline usually succeeds. Historical build success does not establish the source revision, authorization, or destination of this run.
variants.reasoning: Provenance, secret scope, and actual deployment outcomes align with the approved release. The secret’s value was unnecessary for this review.
remaining: Whether the deployment health checks remain satisfactory.
Whether the secret version is rotated according to policy.
variants.next: Attach provenance and deployment identifiers to the review.
variants.pitfall: Treating any successful secret read as a leak.

results: The run executed an unreviewed workflow revision from a lower-trust change context, yet obtained the deployment identity’s secret access.
The job made an unexpected outbound request and produced no artifact matching the approved release. The request metadata does not reveal its body.
The pipeline usually succeeds. Historical build success does not establish the source revision, authorization, or destination of this run.
variants.reasoning: The trust-context mismatch and unexpected job outcomes support escalation for improper secret access. The available egress metadata does not prove the secret value was transmitted.
remaining: Whether sensitive content was included in the outbound request.
How the workload identity binding allowed this run.
variants.next: Review the identity binding and preserve the bounded job records for incident analysis.
variants.pitfall: Claiming secret exfiltration merely from a secret read followed by an outbound request.

results: The job summary names a branch but lacks an immutable revision and workflow digest. Approval records are incomplete.
The completion message cannot be matched to a deployed artifact or target receipt.
The pipeline usually succeeds. Historical build success does not establish the source revision, authorization, or destination of this run.
variants.reasoning: A secret read occurred, but source provenance, authorization context, and actual deployment outcome remain unverified.
remaining: Immutable source and workflow identifiers.
Artifact and deployment receipts.
variants.next: Obtain immutable provenance and target-side deployment evidence.
variants.pitfall: Using a mutable branch name or a job’s own success message as complete verification.

challenge: Which identifiers would make the build and deployment result independently reviewable?
debriefPrinciple: Bind secret use to immutable provenance and verify the resulting environment state.

title: A release artifact was replaced
brief: Assess a changed release artifact by verifying provenance, authorized publication, and downstream adoption.
context: A release registry at {{org}} reports a new digest under an existing release label. The label is convenient for users but does not identify immutable content, and the first packet omits build provenance.

initial.text: At {{time}}, an existing release label was updated to point to a different artifact digest.
The publication used a service identity; the initiating build and approval are not included.
At {{later}}, deployment tooling queried the label, but the alert does not state which digest was actually deployed.

unknowns: Was replacing this label authorized for this release?
Does the new digest match a verified build from approved source?
Which digest did downstream environments actually adopt?
hypotheses: An approved rebuild or corrective release updated the label.
An unapproved artifact was published through the release identity.
Missing provenance and deployment receipts prevent assessment.

checks.label: Read artifact provenance and publication approval
checks.purpose: Match immutable source, build, digest, and approved release action.
checks.scope: The old and new digest, publisher session, and approval {{ticket}}.

checks.label: Read downstream digest receipts
checks.purpose: Determine which artifact bytes were adopted by each in-scope environment.
checks.scope: Deployment receipts for environments that queried this release label.

checks.label: Read the release label’s historical update count
checks.purpose: Provide history without validating the new content.
checks.scope: Label-update metadata only; no artifact execution.

results: The new digest matches a verified build of the reviewed revision, and {{ticket}} explicitly authorizes replacing this release label.
Target-side receipts show the approved new digest in the intended test environment; production remains on its documented prior digest.
The release label has changed in earlier maintenance windows. Previous updates do not authenticate the current digest or authorize this replacement.
variants.reasoning: Publication provenance and target-side adoption match the approved release plan. A matching label alone would not establish the content deployed.
remaining: Whether promotion prerequisites have been met.
Whether any out-of-scope consumer adopted the label.
variants.next: Record the immutable digests and follow the release promotion criteria.
variants.pitfall: Comparing version labels while ignoring artifact digests.

results: The new digest has no matching trusted build provenance, and the publisher session is outside the approved release window.
A production receipt records the new digest despite the approval allowing only the prior digest.
The release label has changed in earlier maintenance windows. Previous updates do not authenticate the current digest or authorize this replacement.
variants.reasoning: Unverified publication and confirmed out-of-scope adoption support escalation. The artifact’s behavior requires separate analysis; provenance failure alone does not identify a payload.
remaining: What changes the new artifact contains.
How the publisher identity was used.
variants.next: Preserve digest-specific evidence and request authorized release incident handling.
variants.pitfall: Calling the artifact malware solely because provenance is missing.

results: The approval refers to a release label but omits an immutable digest, and the build attestation has not been retrieved.
Deployment logs retain the queried label but not the resolved digest or target receipt.
The release label has changed in earlier maintenance windows. Previous updates do not authenticate the current digest or authorize this replacement.
